content.text:
Deze cursus biedt een inleiding in de filosofie van cultuur in drie delen.

1. In het eerste, grootste deel van de cursus bestuderen we de ontwikkeling van de betekenis van het begrip cultuur, vanuit de voorgeschiedenis van het Griekse *paideia*, via het latijnse *cultura* tot het moderne begrip van *Bildung*, aan de hand van primaire teksten van Plato, Aristoteles, Hobbes, Rousseau, Kant, Schiller, Schlegel, Hegel en Comte.
2. In het tweede deel bestuderen we de manier waarop de Bildungsidealen bekritiseerd worden bij Marx, Nietzsche en Freud, en hoe cultuur niet meer vanzelfsprekend de ontwikkeling en hoogste prestaties van de mens uitdrukt, maar nu zelf als problematisch verschijnt (respectievelijk als ideologisch mechanisme; als teken van zwakke of decadente levensvorm; en als repressie van driften).
    Door verschillende ontwikkelingen vindt in de 20e eeuw een significante verbreding van het cultuurbegrip plaats. Cultuur geeft niet meer uitdrukking aan een hoogste mogelijkheid van menselijke ontwikkeling, maar verschillende culturen (in meervoud) kunnen als zelfstandige betekenisvelden naast elkaar bestaan en alles kan als potentieel cultureel significant benaderd worden.
    Deze pluralisering van het cultuurbegrip maakt een grote verscheidenheid van nieuwe benaderingen van cultuur mogelijk (sociologie, antropologie, cultuurwetenschappen, cultural studies, etc.).
3. We eindigen de cursus met drie filosofische kwesties in het licht van dit nieuwe cultuurbegrip: aan de hand van Heideggers werk over techniek bestuderen we waarom cultuur toch niet slechts een contingente *Weltanschauung* kan zijn; met Arendt en Adorno bestuderen we de verticale hiërarchie in het cultuurbegrip (‘hogere’ en ‘lagere’ cultuur, massacultuur en entertainment), en we sluiten af met de vraag hoe cultuur bepaalt wat geldt als “normaal” aan de hand van werk van Raymond Williams en Michel Foucault.

De cursus als geheel raakt meermaals aan, maar focust niet op, cultuur in de betekenis van kunst en esthetica, of normatieve discussies over identiteit, culturele verschillen en cultuurrelativisme. De cursus stelt zich tot doel studenten op een dergelijke vervolgstudie voor te bereiden door de betekenis van het begrip cultuur als zodanig te beschouwen.

### Doelstellingen

Doel van de cursus is studenten in te leiden in de filosofie van cultuur. De cursus focust niet op cultuur in de betekenis van kunst en esthetica, of op normatieve discussies over culturele verschillen en cultuurrelativisme, maar stelt zich tot doel studenten op een dergelijke vervolgstudie voor te bereiden door belangrijke visies op cultuur als zodanig te beschouwen.

### Eindtermen

De student die de cursus succesvol heeft afgerond heeft kennis van:

* de ontwikkeling van filosofische concepties van cultuur;
* belangrijke manieren waarop cultuur als probleem is beschouwd (repressie, crisis, vervreemding, uitsluiting) en hoe cultuur bekritiseerd kan worden.

De student die de cursus succesvol heeft afgerond is in staat om:

* canonieke teksten m.b.t. cultuur te reconstrueren, interpreteren, kritisch te bevragen, en te vergelijken;
* op schrift belangrijke argumenten over cultuur in te brengen en te verdedigen die betrekking hebben op de cursus.

Ethiek tracht inzicht te verschaffen in vragen als ‘hoe te leven?’, ’wat te doen?’ en ‘wat is goed?’. In dit college gaan we na of, en zo ja hoe we antwoorden op deze vragen kunnen rechtvaardigen. We zullen bekijken welke rol waarden, rechten, plichten, deugden, maar ook zaken als karakter en geluk spelen bij de beantwoording van deze vragen. Hierbij zullen we uitgebreid stilstaan bij de meest invloedrijke tradities in de hedendaagse filosofische ethiek, hoe hun antwoorden in elkaar steken, welke rechtvaardigingen ze gebruiken, maar ook voor welke kritieken ze vatbaar (lijken te) zijn.
Naast dat we ingaan op de meest invloedrijke antwoorden en rechtvaardigingen, zullen we ook veel aandacht hebben voor de vraag of het eigenlijk wel mogelijk is om in de ethiek te komen tot goede en slechte antwoorden, of dat de ethiek niet veel meer is dan een kwestie van subjectieve gevoelens.

De student die de cursus succesvol heeft afgerond heeft kennis van:

* De student kent de volgende begrippen en onderscheidingen en kan ethische opvattingen in deze termen beschrijven: waarde, plicht, deugd, consequentialisme, utilisme, deontologie, deugdethiek, realisme, anti-realisme, cognitivisme, non-cognitivisme, naturalisme, relativisme.
* De student kan in hoofdlijnen de ethische theorieën van Aristoteles, Kant en Mill beschrijven en ook de centrale punten van de bestudeerde teksten weergeven en herkennen.

De student die de cursus succesvol heeft afgerond is in staat om:

* Deze begrippen met elkaar in verband te brengen en zowel mondeling als schriftelijk te gebruiken in eenvoudige filosofische redeneringen binnen de ethiek.
* Zelfstandig niet al te moeilijke artikelen op het gebied der ethiek te bestuderen en begrijpen.
* In groepsverband samen te werken aan filosofische vraagstukken en opdrachten.

De epistemologie of kennisleer is de tak van de filosofie die zich richt op de aard, oorsprong en rechtvaardiging van kennis. Wat kunnen wij weten, en hoe weten wij dat wij het weten? In deze inleidende cursus maken studenten kennis met de centrale thema’s en vragen van de epistemologie: Wat is kennis? Wat betekent het dat een bewering waar is? Is alle kennis gebaseerd op zintuiglijke ervaring (empirisme), of bestaan er ook vormen van a priori-kennis (rationalisme)? Kunnen inductieve redeneringen gerechtvaardigd worden? Wat houdt filosofisch scepticisme precies in, en hoe zou men daar filosofisch op moeten reageren? Aan de hand van zowel klassieke en hedendaagse bijdragen worden uiteenlopende theorieën over kennis systematisch besproken. Hoewel de epistemologie vele benaderingen kent, blijven bepaalde fundamentele problemen hardnekkig onopgelost. Studenten worden uitgenodigd actief mee te denken over mogelijke oplossingen, en zo hun eigen filosofisch inzicht en analytische vaardigheden verder te ontwikkelen.

Deze cursus biedt een heldere en gestructureerde introductie op filosofie behorend tot de zogenaamde ‘continentale’ traditie vanaf de tweede helft van de 20e eeuw. Denkers als Heidegger, Arendt, Sartre, De Beauvoir, Marcuse, Lacan, Deleuze, Foucault, Derrida, Butler en Žižek grepen terug op de ideeën van o.a. Kant, Hegel, Marx, Nietzsche en Freud en ontwikkelden radicale kritieken op traditioneel-filosofische opvattingen over kennis en het menselijk subject. Aan bod komen onderwerpen als het belang van historisch of ‘genealogisch’ denken, identiteit en verschil, de rol van macht en filosofische maatschappijkritiek, en het belang van vrijheid.

Normative ethics concerns that part of ethics that deals with the traditional, substantial ethical questions such as ‘How should one live?’ and ‘What should I do?’ Ethical theories as utilitarianism, kantianism, contractualism and virtue ethics propose a different sets of answers to these questions. Often those answers are reduced down to a principle that is meant to organize, unify and justify various moral judgments. Constructing normative ethics as a search for a principle is telling of how ethical theories imagine normative ethics works. In this course, we study these theories and the way they use principles. We will discuss and assess whether different ethical theories offer different understandings of normative ethics, and question whether it makes good sense to understand normative ethics as a search for a principle or a theory.

There are 8 billion people alive in the world. The quality of their lives varies greatly depending where they live, as do the opportunities they have to achieve things they have reason to value and the way they are treated by those who rule them. This course brings the resources of moral and political philosophy to the key questions of understanding and action: What is wrong with this state of affairs, and what should we do about it?
 
In the first part of the course we investigate key themes of global justice such as relating to climate change, international aid, trade, and migration. In the second part we focus on the most influential paradigm of global justice: human rights.

Students who successfully complete the course will have a good understanding of:

•	Key ideas and arguments about global justice developed by ethicists and political philosophers.

Students who successfully complete the course will be able to:

•	Critically evaluate the ideas, arguments of the authors studied, as well as debates between them
•	Apply the philosophical resources studied to real-world problems.

concepts: Retain three genuine qualified philosophy responses. Each shares five PHIL courses37.5EC; political philosophy, human rights philosophy, AI ethics and formal logic add genuine philosophical contributions rather than merely adjacent context. First organises intellectual/cultural interpretation; second prioritises institutions, rights, justice and critical social theory; third develops mind/language/science with empirical and computational complements. Their actual different curricula, not titles alone, support distinctness. No equivalent specialist historical/epistemological/science/language sequence or required philosophy thesis claimed. Maximum three reached sequentially; no default quota used.

courses.actualSubject: Develops academic writing and research-literacy skills alongside personal development and civic engagement. Students locate and evaluate scholarly sources, synthesize literature, formulate research questions and arguments, and construct a research-paper introduction. A community-engaged project with a societal partner connects these skills to collaboration, reflection and practical contribution. Personal development planning addresses learning goals, self-efficacy, and stress and time management; the course also considers responsible academic use of AI.
courses.methods: Scholarly literature searching and source evaluation; Literature synthesis; CARS model for research introductions; Reflective development planning; Community project co-design
courses.rationale: Required PPD; not counted as philosophy.

courses.role: direct philosophical subject or formal method
courses.actualSubject: Examines AI through ethical theory and psychological accounts of human behaviour and interaction. Ethical debates address fairness, privacy, responsibility, alignment, moral status and political or existential risks. Psychological perspectives consider development, clinical care, social and organizational relationships, forensic applications and cognitive neuroscience. Students synthesize literature and apply ethical frameworks in an analytical psychology project and a research-grounded podcast, with a creative communication component.
courses.methods: Ethical-framework application; Philosophical argument evaluation; Psychological-literature synthesis; Theory-based analysis of AI applications; Research podcast scripting, recording and editing
courses.rationale: applies ethical reasoning to artificial intelligence, agency and responsibility

courses.role: direct philosophical subject or formal method
courses.actualSubject: Introduces formal logic, abstract mathematical reasoning and proof. Students analyze propositions and quantified statements, work with sets, Boolean algebra, functions and relations, and develop direct and indirect proofs. Induction and recursive definitions extend these tools to mathematical structures. The final component systematically models processes and games without chance and investigates the existence and construction of winning strategies.
courses.methods: Truth-table analysis; Direct proof and proof by cases; Proof by contrapositive and contradiction; Proof with quantifiers; Mathematical induction; Formal process and game modelling
courses.rationale: develops formal logic and discrete reasoning relevant to valid argument and representation

courses.actualSubject: Introduces statistical learning for understanding data and predicting outcomes. Students study regression and classification, model accuracy, resampling, regularization, nonlinear models, trees, support vector machines and unsupervised learning. Practical assignments evaluate methods on real data using R or Python. Projects emphasize informative predictor construction, test-set prediction, appropriate model choice and clear reporting of results and limitations.
courses.methods: Linear and logistic regression; Generative classification; Cross-validation and bootstrap; Subset selection; Ridge regression and LASSO; Splines and generalized additive models; Basic and advanced decision-tree methods; Support vector machines; Principal component analysis; Clustering; Predictive-performance evaluation; R or Python implementation
courses.rationale: examines machine learning as a concrete model of artificial inference and intelligent behaviour

courses.actualSubject: Introduces computational problem-solving and programming in Python. Students develop structured programs using branching, iteration, functions and data collections, then progress to recursion, exception handling and object-oriented programming with inheritance. Elements of logic, sets and enumeration support computational reasoning. Exercises and projects require students to write, trace, test, debug and explain programs that solve problems of moderate complexity.
courses.methods: Structured programming in Python; Object-oriented programming; Recursive problem-solving; Program tracing; Testing and debugging; Exception handling
courses.rationale: provides computational foundations for examining artificial systems and representation

courses.actualSubject: Introduces law through legal, social and normative perspectives. Students compare major legal traditions and survey public and private law, including constitutional, criminal, international, human-rights, property, contract and tort law. The second part examines justice, social control and change, race and gender. Case briefs, legal interpretation, demand letters and mock trials apply legal reasoning; a family-law topic supports the design of a small socio-legal research proposal.
courses.methods: Legal interpretation; Case-law research and IRAC case briefing; Demand-letter drafting; Mock-trial legal argumentation; Socio-legal research design; Literature review
courses.rationale: introduces law, social order and competing conceptions of justice

courses.actualSubject: Surveys economic, political and cultural developments from 1815 to the present while questioning the meaning and periodization of modernity. Students examine industrialization, political ideologies, nationalism, imperialism, migration, world wars, revolution, decolonization, the Cold War and globalization. Historical research and essays connect specific questions to evidence. A group project analyzes historical visions of the future as products of their own contexts and compares them with subsequent developments.
courses.methods: Historical contextualization; Primary- and secondary-source analysis; Source triangulation; Historical research-question development
courses.rationale: situates modern philosophical and political ideas in historical change

courses.actualSubject: Studies gendered histories and lives in North America from the nineteenth century to the present, centering storytelling and intersectionality. Queer and heteronormative narratives connect slavery, family, sexuality, health, incarceration and contemporary backlash to resistance and activism. Students interpret primary sources and scholarship, interview older queer people, contribute to the Walking with Pride activist artwork, and conduct an original research project in a chosen format.
courses.methods: Historical primary-source research; Intersectional analysis; Oral-history interviewing; Critical interpretation of memoir and cultural representations; Arts-based research; Community-engaged activist art; Reflective analysis
courses.rationale: traces gendered identities and marginalisation through historical interpretation

courses.actualSubject: Studies Native American social and cultural histories from the nineteenth century to the present through Indigenous perspectives and collaborative inquiry. Boarding schools, institutional violence, family separation and intergenerational trauma are connected to contemporary resistance, resurgence, food sovereignty and cultural expression. Storytelling, relational accountability and reciprocity inform work with Indigenous peers and knowledge holders. Arts-based collaborations and a public-history project develop respectful, accessible accounts of historical and contemporary issues.
courses.methods: Indigenous storywork and relational historical inquiry; Primary-source and oral-history analysis; Arts-based collaborative inquiry; Photo/Voice photography and audio narratives; Historical contextualization of contemporary issues; Public-history multimedia production
courses.rationale: examines Indigenous-centred histories, colonial knowledge and marginalised perspectives

courses.role: direct philosophical subject or formal method
courses.actualSubject: Studies human rights both as positive law and as philosophical claims. Students examine the UDHR, European and UN protection systems, monitoring institutions and landmark cases alongside natural law, natural rights, legal positivism and critiques of universality. Historical and philosophical texts frame debates about dignity, life and reproductive rights, punishment, religious freedom, expression and democracy. Close engagement with legal and philosophical arguments supports independent moral positions.
courses.methods: Treaty and legal-text analysis; Judicial and treaty-body case-law research; Case-law analysis; Philosophical text and argument analysis
courses.rationale: examines philosophical foundations and legal expression of human rights

courses.actualSubject: Examines the principles of criminal liability and the legal and moral bases of criminal justice. Students study criminal acts, causation and mental elements, legality, punishment, criminalization, justifications, excuses, inchoate offences and participation. A simulated legal-aid clinic applies doctrine to hypothetical facts through advice memoranda and oral argument. A criminology or organized-crime research proposal develops a literature review and methodology.
courses.methods: Comparative criminal-law analysis; Case-law analysis; Application of legal principles to hypothetical facts; Legal-advice memorandum writing; Simulated legal-aid argumentation; Criminological research design and literature review
courses.rationale: studies responsibility, punishment and justice through criminal law

courses.actualSubject: Compares constitutional structures, institutions and rights across legal systems and introduces administrative law. Students examine constitutional features, federalism, legislatures, executive relationships, courts, judicial review and human rights. The administrative component addresses public participation, remedies and procedural fairness. A staged booklet compares two constitutions, supported by legal interpretation, case-law analysis and application of principles to hypothetical facts.
courses.methods: Comparative constitutional analysis; Constitutional and legislative interpretation; Case-law analysis; Application of legal principles to hypothetical facts; Structured comparative legal writing
courses.rationale: compares constitutional arrangements, rights and distributions of political authority

courses.actualSubject: Introduces the EU legal order through its institutions, sources, competences and relationship to member-state law. Students study supremacy, legal effect, liability and judicial remedies before applying citizenship and free-movement law to concrete problems. Structured legal cases and research into current judgments develop interpretation and comparison across EU and domestic settings. Digital regulation and the green transition provide a contemporary application.
courses.methods: EU legal-source research; Case-law analysis; Comparative interpretation of EU and national law; Application of free-movement principles to factual scenarios; Structured legal problem analysis
courses.rationale: examines the legal and institutional foundations of European political order

courses.role: direct philosophical subject or formal method
courses.actualSubject: Introduces major philosophical questions through close study of arguments from ancient Greek thought to contemporary philosophy, with a related Buddhist perspective on the self. Students examine knowledge, ethics, God, mind and consciousness, freedom, identity, time and meaning. Historical texts and contemporary debates, including AI consciousness and concepts of race and gender, develop the ability to reconstruct, evaluate and formulate philosophical arguments in focused essays.
courses.methods: Close reading of philosophical texts; Conceptual analysis; Philosophical argument reconstruction and evaluation; Argumentative essay development
courses.rationale: provides the broad disciplinary entry point to Western philosophical questions and traditions

courses.role: direct philosophical subject or formal method
courses.actualSubject: Studies moral reasoning through historical and contemporary ethical theories and close philosophical reading. Utilitarianism, consequentialism, Kantian ethics, virtue ethics, contractarianism and feminist ethics lead into Nietzsche's genealogy, Murdoch's account of goodness and Nagel's treatments of value, perspective, death and meaning. Reflection and research essays require interpretation, argument evaluation and an independent position on ethical theory or a practical ethical problem.
courses.methods: Close philosophical text analysis; Reconstruction and critical evaluation of moral arguments; Comparison of ethical theories; Conceptual analysis; Independent philosophical argument development
courses.rationale: examines ethical theories, duties, rights and moral responsibility

courses.role: direct philosophical subject or formal method
courses.actualSubject: Examines minds, selves and conscious experience through historical and contemporary philosophy. Personal identity and self-knowledge are considered alongside Buddhist accounts and neuropsychological cases. Behaviourism, physicalism, functionalism and their critics frame the mind-body problem. Later inquiries address machine consciousness, virtual worlds, dreaming, perception, transformative experience and the value of experience. Essays develop independent philosophical interpretations and arguments.
courses.methods: Close philosophical reading; Conceptual analysis; Reconstruction and evaluation of arguments; Comparison of theories of mind; Literature-based philosophical research
courses.rationale: studies consciousness, personal identity and the relation between mind and world

courses.role: direct philosophical subject or formal method
courses.actualSubject: Examines what emotions are and how they shape knowledge, decision-making, ethics, social life and politics. Feeling, cognitive and perceptual theories are compared with historical, phenomenological and contemporary accounts. Love, fear, grief, moods and political anger provide focused cases, alongside emotions in art and their changing relation to time. Students analyze texts and emotional vignettes and develop an independent philosophical paper or a project combining argument with creative work.
courses.methods: Close philosophical reading; Conceptual and argumentative analysis; Phenomenological description of emotional experience; Critical comparison of emotion theories
courses.rationale: examines emotion, rationality and human experience as philosophy of mind

courses.role: direct philosophical subject or formal method
courses.actualSubject: Explores free will and agency in relation to time and the self. Historical Greek and Indian perspectives introduce debates about fatalism, determinism, compatibility and moral responsibility; later topics include scientific challenges, addiction, luck and agency in games. The second part examines the reality and experience of time, physics and temporal asymmetries, then developing research linking time, action and selfhood. Essays require close source analysis and an independent argument.
courses.methods: Conceptual analysis; Close philosophical reading; Argument reconstruction and evaluation; Literature-based philosophical research
courses.rationale: investigates free will, time, agency and the self

courses.role: direct philosophical subject or formal method
courses.actualSubject: Surveys political thought from classical antiquity to contemporary debates, including European and non-European thinkers. Students examine views of human nature, society, rights and authority in their historical contexts and compare their proposed solutions with current political problems. Close study of original texts, an individual essay and a group project developing a coherent political philosophy connect historical interpretation to normative argument.
courses.methods: Political-text interpretation; Historical contextualization of political ideas; Comparative political argument analysis; Assumption identification; Normative political-theory construction
courses.rationale: develops normative arguments about political power, justice and political life

courses.actualSubject: Introduces empirical comparison of political systems, with democracy, democratization and autocratization as central concerns. Students study political institutions, rules, actors and behaviour, including parties, elections, participation, polarization, interest groups and policy. Research exercises operationalize and measure democracy using V-Dem data and compare academic literature-search tools. A qualitative or quantitative research memo answers a theoretically grounded comparative-politics question through empirical analysis.
courses.methods: Theory-driven qualitative and quantitative research; Concept operationalization and democracy measurement; V-Dem data analysis; Comparative case analysis; Academic literature searching with OpenAlex and AI tools; Empirical election analysis; Research-question formulation
courses.rationale: provides comparative frameworks for political institutions and power

courses.actualSubject: Introduces international relations and geopolitics through competing theoretical approaches and historical and contemporary cases. Students study realism, liberalism, Marxism, constructivism, critical theory and foreign-policy analysis. Case research connects theories to conflicts, colonial relationships, economic competition and climate politics. A UN Security Council simulation requires country-position research, strategy and position papers, negotiation and collaborative resolution drafting.
courses.methods: Theory-guided international case analysis; Historical-source analysis; Comparative foreign-policy analysis; Country-position and strategy research; Diplomatic negotiation simulation; Position-paper and resolution drafting
courses.rationale: tests political theories, norms and explanatory arguments in international relations

courses.actualSubject: Studies EU institutions, political actors, integration and policymaking, linking formal rules to current political issues. Students analyze representation, legitimacy, interests, agenda setting, decision-making and implementation. A substantial empirical project examines European Parliament committee amendments, connecting MEP ideology and possible interest-group influence to amendment activity. Students develop a project plan, code amendments, assess salience and trace legislative processes.
courses.methods: EU policy and legislative-document research; Process tracing; Systematic amendment coding; Ideology and amendment-activity analysis; Salience assessment; Comparative news-source analysis
courses.rationale: examines political institutions, authority and choices in European governance

courses.actualSubject: Investigates public policy in the context of globalization. Uses a case study on sugar to examine policy‑making phases and alternative conceptualisations across national and international arenas. Students write policy memos.
courses.rationale: examines policy-making phases, alternative policy concepts and decisions across global, national and international arenas

courses.actualSubject: Examines causes and dynamics of conflict and approaches to peace through legal, sociological, political and historical perspectives. Structural inequality, identity and colonial legacies are connected to international security, humanitarian law, human rights, peacebuilding and transitional justice. Students compare travelling concepts across disciplines, produce an interdisciplinary podcast, and develop an evidence-based policy brief with a research dossier. Positionality reflection addresses how assumptions shape inquiry.
courses.methods: Interdisciplinary Research Process; Cross-disciplinary travelling-concept analysis; Conflict case analysis; Context and stakeholder mapping; Annotated bibliography and evidence synthesis; Policy-option appraisal; Policy-brief and background-dossier development; Researcher positionality analysis; Comparative research podcast production
courses.rationale: asks how conflict arises and how peacebuilding may be justified

courses.actualSubject: Develops qualitative inquiry from research design and preparation through data collection, management, analysis and dissemination. Students examine methodological foundations, ethics, positionality and reflexivity alongside interviews, focus groups, ethnography, documentary and visual approaches. Coding, thematic interpretation and NVivo support analysis. Research teams formulate a question, collect and analyze qualitative evidence, and report their methodological decisions, findings and limitations in staged assignments.
courses.methods: Qualitative research design; Interviews; Focus groups; Ethnography and participant observation; Documentary and archival analysis; Visual-data analysis; Participatory video and drawing; Transcription; Qualitative coding; Thematic analysis; NVivo-supported analysis; Reflexive methodological evaluation
courses.rationale: provides qualitative interpretive methods for investigating contemporary social questions

courses.actualSubject: Examines twentieth-century and contemporary social theory alongside critical accounts of modernity, colonialism and disciplinary exclusion. Functionalism, critical theory, Black feminist thought, phenomenology, symbolic interactionism and Bourdieu's work are read with postcolonial, decolonial and Indigenous perspectives. Students compare theories and apply them to empirical cases, including visual material. An individual research paper develops a theoretically grounded interpretation of a selected social phenomenon.
courses.methods: Close reading of social theory; Comparative theoretical analysis; Theory-guided empirical case analysis; Visual sociological analysis; Literature-based sociological research
courses.rationale: adds major modern social theories for analysing institutions and social change

courses.actualSubject: Focuses on social movement theories and environmental justice. Uses case studies from the Environmental Justice Atlas and integrates perspectives such as feminism, anti‑colonialism, degrowth and environmental peacebuilding to encourage civic engagement.
courses.rationale: examines collective action, environmental justice and marginalisation

courses.courseName: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory
courses.actualSubject: Focuses on civil society through critical, neo-functionalist and decolonial social theory. Students examine social trust, capital, hegemony, public spheres, solidarity, social movements and civil repair across political and regional contexts. An experience report relates personal engagement or observation to course concepts. An individual research project uses theoretical and empirical sources to analyze a civil-society organization, movement, initiative or related phenomenon.
courses.methods: Comparative social-theory analysis; Theory-guided empirical case analysis; Document and secondary-source analysis; Structured reflection on civil-society engagement or observation; Sociological research design
courses.rationale: uses contemporary social theory to interpret identity, power and emerging social problems

courses.actualSubject: Studies nervous systems and behaviour from comparative, evolutionary and physiological perspectives. Brain anatomy and laboratory introductions support analysis of animal behaviour, research models and welfare. The second part connects regulatory behaviour and biological rhythms to sleep, lifestyle drugs, mood and eating disorders. Comparative-anatomy work and a literature-based disorder report apply neurobiological concepts while animal-research assignments examine reduction, refinement and replacement.
courses.methods: Comparative brain-anatomy analysis; Introductory microscopy and cell staining; Brain-model comparison; Ethical appraisal of animal research and the 3Rs; Literature-based analysis of neurobiological disorders
courses.rationale: grounds questions about mind and representation in neural systems

courses.actualSubject: Explores neural mechanisms behind perception and action. Examines how the brain processes sensory information and guides goal‑directed behaviour using methods from cognitive neuroscience and neuropsychology.
courses.rationale: studies how perception and action connect mental representation to the world

courses.actualSubject: Deepens understanding of neuroanatomy, neurophysiology and the experimental study of higher cognitive functions. Students examine attention, memory, emotion, cognitive control, social cognition, pain and consciousness, connecting brain function and dysfunction to behaviour. An attentional-blink experiment provides direct engagement with empirical work. A team research proposal requires literature analysis, a feasible experimental design and ethical reflection, supported by peer review.
courses.methods: Cognitive-neuroscience experimental design; Attentional-blink experiment; Critical analysis of scientific literature and empirical data; Research-proposal development; Scientific peer review
courses.rationale: studies advanced cognition and higher-order mental functions

courses.actualSubject: Psycholinguistics is the study of the neurobiological and psychological factors that enable us to acquire, use, and understand language. Modern research draws on cognitive psychology, neuroscience, and computer science to investigate how language is processed. The course focuses primarily, though not exclusively, on the neuroscience of language. Students examine theoretical and experimental issues in speech production and comprehension, language impairments, the relationship between thought and language, and the evolution and acquisition of language. They also gain hands-on experience with experimental approaches to the study of language and develop an understanding of human linguistic capacity as a subject of multidisciplinary research. Topics covered: What is language? Evolutionary aspects of language and animal communication; language and thought; aphasia; language acquisition; bilingualism; speech comprehension; semantics; reading and dyslexia; speech production.
courses.rationale: examines the relation between language processing, cognition and the brain

courses.actualSubject: Introduces psychological and neuroscientific explanations of behaviour and mental processes. Students study neural signalling, brain anatomy and development, learning, intelligence, personality, social influence, mental disorders and treatments. Several sessions introduce behavioural, imaging and electrophysiological approaches to neuroscience and their combined use. Interdisciplinary research-article and case analysis connects psychological processes to neural mechanisms and clinical questions.
courses.methods: Psychological and neuroscientific research appraisal; Interdisciplinary case-study analysis
courses.rationale: introduces brain, behaviour and cognition as empirical perspectives on mind and human nature

courses.actualSubject: Introduces the scientific study of how thoughts, feelings and behaviour are shaped by other people and social situations. Social cognition, the self, influence and persuasion lead into group processes, prejudice, aggression, prosocial behaviour, attraction and close relationships. Students critically examine empirical research, synthesize findings from journal articles, formulate theory-guided questions and design a feasible study. The final project proposes research rather than conducting an empirical investigation.
courses.methods: Critical appraisal of empirical social-psychology research; Literature synthesis; Theory-guided hypothesis formulation; Research design for a proposed social-psychology study
courses.rationale: examines how persons think and act in social contexts

courses.actualSubject: Develops experimental-design knowledge and practical statistical analysis for health and behavioural research. Students choose, fit, diagnose and interpret multivariable models, comparing means, analyzing categorical outcomes and studying latent constructs. R, primarily through R Commander, supports repeated practical exercises; SPSS is an optional alternative. Data-analysis papers and a poster connect research questions and hypotheses to appropriate models, assumption checks, substantive interpretation and APA reporting.
courses.methods: R and R Commander data analysis; Multiple linear regression and dummy coding; Regression diagnostics; t-tests and nonparametric alternatives; ANOVA and ANCOVA; Factorial, repeated-measures and mixed-design ANOVA; Logistic regression; Exploratory factor analysis; Principal component analysis; Cronbach's alpha; APA statistical reporting
courses.rationale: develops experimental and statistical methods for claims about mind and behaviour

courses.actualSubject: Teaches systematic review and meta-analysis for synthesizing evidence in medical, behavioural and related research. Students define review questions, search and select studies, extract and code findings, assess bias and compute effect sizes. Hands-on R work fits fixed- and random-effects models, examines heterogeneity and moderators, conducts meta-regression and investigates publication bias. A group project completes a small meta-analysis and presents its methods and results in a research poster.
courses.methods: Systematic literature review; Database searching and study screening; Study-data extraction and coding; Critical risk-of-bias appraisal; R programming and data management; Effect-size calculation and conversion; Fixed- and random-effects meta-analysis; Moderator and subgroup analysis; Meta-regression; Publication-bias analysis; Meta-analytic visualization and reporting
courses.rationale: develops systematic review and meta-analysis skills, including bias assessment, effect sizes and analysis in R

courses.actualSubject: Teaches rhetorical analysis and persuasive communication through classical history, theory and practice. Students study Greek and Roman rhetoric, the five canons, types of discourse, persuasive appeals, argumentation and fallacies. Written exercises, debates and public speeches develop invention, arrangement, style, memory and delivery. An applied project creates narrative and storytelling material for an immersive educational setting concerned with Zeeland's climate and community.
courses.methods: Rhetorical text analysis; Stasis analysis; Argument invention and arrangement; Stylistic analysis and composition; Structured debate; Persuasive speechwriting and delivery; Educational storytelling design
courses.rationale: trains the analysis and construction of persuasive arguments

courses.actualSubject: Studies how linguistic choices produce meaning and interpretive effects, principally in literary texts but also in nonfiction. Students connect linguistic description to interpretation across grammar, discourse and cognition. Stylistic frameworks address foregrounding, dialogue, narration, modality, transitivity, deixis, schemas, construal and text worlds. Frequent analysis exercises lead to an original, research-supported stylistic analysis of a selected text.
courses.methods: Linguistic stylistic analysis; Close textual analysis; Discourse and conversation analysis; Speech and thought presentation analysis; Modality and transitivity analysis; Deictic and cognitive-grammar analysis; Text-world analysis; Framework-based interpretation supported by retrievable textual evidence
courses.rationale: Studies how linguistic choices shape literary meaning through stylistic and text-world analysis; a specific interpretive complement, not analytic philosophy of naming/reference.

courses.actualSubject: Applies rhetoric through community-engaged work with local primary-school children. Students develop their own public-speaking, debating and storytelling skills, then design and iteratively refine age-appropriate teaching activities with school partners. On-site coaching and a final public-speaking event connect rhetorical education to civic participation and confidence. Structured reflection examines reciprocity, cultural sensitivity, personal development and the practical challenges of community-engaged teaching.
courses.methods: Public-speaking and debate coaching; Storytelling exercises; Iterative design and revision of teaching materials; Practice-based rhetorical instruction; Gibbs reflective-cycle analysis; Public-speaking event design and evaluation
courses.rationale: Applies rhetoric through public-speaking and debate coaching with primary-school partners, including reflective community-engaged educational work; a practical communication complement, not advanced moral philosophy.

courses.actualSubject: Examines contemporary persuasion through communication studies, social psychology and ethical analysis, then applies it in community-engaged work. Students study coactive persuasion, framing, argumentation, cognitive shortcuts and verbal and nonverbal communication. Projects with the Delta Climate Centre and Vlissingen municipality develop communication encouraging sustainable and circular lifestyles. An individual research paper evaluates selected persuasion tools through literature review, field research diaries and reflective analysis of their use.
courses.methods: Persuasive-message design; Communication consulting and implementation; Literature review; Qualitative research diaries; Action research; Reflective case-study analysis; Gibbs reflective cycle
courses.rationale: studies persuasive framing, cognitive shortcuts and ethical influence

courses.actualSubject: Examines how making objects shaped communities and identities from the Neolithic through antiquity across Europe, Asia and Africa. Artefacts, production technologies and craft organization are interpreted in relation to social status, religion, gender, exchange and environmental settings. Students produce an archaeological catalogue description and technical drawings, research a craft-related question and design a hands-on educational game. A small contemporary-archaeology project collects local material evidence and proposes a testable interpretation.
courses.methods: Artefact observation, measurement and cataloguing; Archaeological technical drawing; Visual and stylistic analysis; Comparative material-culture analysis; Archaeological database and literature research; Material-evidence-based argumentation; Archaeological educational-game design; Contemporary archaeological data collection and hypothesis development
courses.rationale: adds ancient and intercultural material contexts to the history of ideas

courses.actualSubject: Studies Athenian democracy through history, archaeology, literature, art and religion, including its exclusions and moments of crisis. Students analyze citizenship, social divisions, myth, ritual and cultural expression through primary texts and material evidence. A historically grounded assembly simulation explores political decision-making. Research reports connect ancient democracy to the present, while a collective cultural project for Middelburg experiments with participatory democratic collaboration.
courses.methods: Primary-text and archaeological-evidence analysis; Historical character research; CREATE reading method; Historically grounded assembly simulation; Ancient-modern comparative analysis; Participatory cultural-project design
courses.rationale: connects ancient democracy, heritage and contested political interpretation

courses.actualSubject: Introduces practical criticism and literary interpretation through fiction, poetry, drama and contemporary nonfiction, with an introductory component on film adaptation. Students investigate literary value and the constructed character of texts, using concepts of plot, character, setting, point of view, symbolism, style and form. Close reading and engagement with critical sources support analytical presentations and an essay or extended book review.
courses.methods: Close reading; Formalist literary analysis; Narrative analysis; Poetic and dramatic analysis; Critical-source integration; Literary essay and review construction
courses.rationale: introduces theories and methods for interpreting language, texts and meaning

courses.actualSubject: Surveys major literary works from ancient epic to modern and later fiction, connecting literary form to questions of humanity, mortality, gender, freedom, community and civilization. Students compare genres and recurring motifs through works including Gilgamesh, Greek tragedy, confessional writing, framed tales, philosophical satire, colonial narratives and modernist fiction. Text-focused analysis and engagement with criticism develop interpretation of theme, technique and cultural context.
courses.methods: Close literary reading; Formalist analysis of genre, theme and technique; Comparative textual interpretation; Narrative analysis; Critical-source interpretation and integration
courses.rationale: uses close reading across periods to strengthen interpretation of major texts and ideas

courses.actualSubject: Compares mythic narratives across ancient and later literary traditions, examining transmission, cultural connections and themes of creation, power, gender, love and loyalty. Greek, Roman, Near Eastern, Indian, Arabic and African materials support comparisons of narrative patterns and representations. Students apply theories of myth and literary analysis in a research paper and graphic explanation, then creatively retell an Ovidian story using another cultural narrative model.
courses.methods: Comparative myth analysis; Structuralist narrative analysis and Propp's motifemes; Focalization analysis; Gender-focused literary analysis; Primary-source and scholarly-literature research; Cross-cultural narrative adaptation
courses.rationale: compares world myths and intellectual traditions as material for intercultural reflection

courses.actualSubject: Examines how different perspectives—humanist, feminist, Marxist, cultural minority and psychoanalytic—affect reading and interpretation. Students undertake a research project applying selected perspectives to texts.
courses.rationale: examines theories of meaning and interpretation through close reading

alignments.reason: Both introduce foundational Western philosophical traditions, including ancient thinkers; UCR is a broader historical survey.

Both study justification of moral judgments through major ethical theories, including consequentialist, Kantian and virtue traditions, using philosophical texts and arguments. Leiden also develops explicit metaethical distinctions.
Both introduce major political-philosophical concepts and arguments; UCR is thematic rather than a dedicated historical survey.
Both examine justice and rights beyond the state; UCR approaches the topic through human-rights law and philosophy.

The current Leiden course studies Islamic moral philosophy, self-cultivation and practical wisdom. The selected UCR courses offer related ethical reasoning but do not reproduce this specialised tradition.

Both critically read modern social thought about subjectivity, power, identity and social criticism. UCR Modern Sociology includes critical, phenomenological and decolonial perspectives; it is a partial social-theory relationship, not the full philosophical canon.

Both examine critical social theory and political agency in historically shaped social relations. UCR centres civil society, hegemony, solidarity and public spheres; Leiden centres dialectical materialism and Marxist/phenomenological political philosophy. The relationship is partial.
Philosophy of Mind addresses knowledge, representation and mental states, covering part of Leiden’s broader epistemology component.
Both examine selfhood, time, agency and free will as metaphysical questions; UCR is a focused advanced seminar.
Both develop formal reasoning and validity; UCR combines logic with discrete mathematics and computing applications.
Both develop argument analysis, academic reasoning, writing, oral communication and critical engagement with claims.

UCR Ethics includes normative theories but is placed with the stronger foundational Ethics relationship. Its credits are not counted a second time against this advanced study of principles and their criticism.
The selected UCR courses do not directly cover this Leiden component’s specific philosophical subject or educational function; it remains a visible curricular difference.
The selected UCR courses do not directly cover this Leiden component’s specific philosophical subject or educational function; it remains a visible curricular difference.
General modern history does not directly teach the philosophical arguments and texts of this history-of-philosophy component.

General historical or policy research is not a sufficient subject-specific counterpart to the required independent philosophy thesis. Optional independent research is shown separately from the scheduled curriculum.
Literary close reading and a cross-period canon do not establish study of medieval philosophical doctrines or arguments.
International-relations explanatory theories do not adequately represent this specialist normative political-philosophy component.
Stylistic analysis of literary meaning is distinct from the analytic philosophical questions of naming, reference and necessity.
Primary-school rhetorical instruction and public-speaking practice are distinct from advanced moral and political philosophy.
Literary theories of meaning and interpretation do not reproduce the specific modern philosophical sequence.
Qualitative data-collection and analysis skills do not by themselves constitute philosophy of science or philosophical inquiry into scientific knowledge.

Leiden traces culture and Bildung through primary philosophical texts and critiques of cultural ideals. Emotion, literary interpretation and historical context are related but do not establish this primary philosophical subject.

alignmentFinding: Reviewed all23 comparator components against the fixed46-code union. Preserve eight earlier weak-match removals, current real policy contribution and explicit optional15EC research outside180. New source-specific reassessment puts Ethics with foundational Ethics, acknowledges partial continental social theory relationships and removes Emotion/Culture association. Meaningful partial relationships do not require equivalence; absence of a full disciplinary replica is not alone a reason for blanks. Remaining blanks concern unsupported primary philosophical subjects or credits already counted with a stronger component. Descriptive epistemology/self-knowledge and rhetorical argument skills receive clear scope notes.
